title: Job 20:1–11
context: Zophar the Naamathite speaks in his second speech, stung by what he calls “the reproof which puts me to shame,” he appeals to what has been known since man was placed on earth: “the triumphing of the wicked is short.” He pictures the wicked rising high and then vanishing like a dream, his children seeking favor from the poor and his strength lying down in the dust. This is Zophar’s view, not the book’s settled doctrine; both traditions agree that God judges evil, while noting that the LORD later says the three friends “have not spoken of me the thing that is right” (42:7).

verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Zophar the Naamathite answered.” Arminian readers note that this is Zophar’s second speech (cf. ch. 11) and, as the book stands, his last.

His words should be read as one voice in a debate, not as the narrator’s verdict.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the friends’ speeches as human arguments that the book will later weigh.

Shared ground: both traditions name the speaker carefully and let the whole book shape how Zophar’s speech is received.

verses.text: “Therefore my thoughts answer me, even by reason of my haste that is in me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says, “Therefore my thoughts answer me, even by reason of my haste that is in me.” Arminian readers note that he admits to an inner urgency driving his reply.

His haste is part of the portrait of a comforter who speaks before he has listened.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a speaker moved by agitation rather than calm reflection.

Shared ground: both traditions draw the pastoral lesson that hurried answers to suffering can wound, whatever truth they contain (cf. James 1:19).

verses.text: I have heard the reproof which puts me to shame. The spirit of my understanding answers me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I have heard the reproof which puts me to shame.” Arminian readers note that Zophar feels insulted by Job’s words, perhaps his warning in 19:28–29.

The text does not say exactly which words he means.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see personal offense shaping Zophar’s reply.

Shared ground: both traditions note that he claims, “The spirit of my understanding answers me,” and both read that claim as his own, to be tested by the rest of the book.

verses.text: Don’t you know this from old time, since man was placed on earth,
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar asks, “Don’t you know this from old time, since man was placed on earth,” and goes on to state his principle. Arminian readers note his appeal to long tradition, as Bildad did (8:8–10).

Tradition carries real wisdom but can be applied too rigidly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise value inherited wisdom while recognizing that the friends misapply it to Job.

Shared ground: both traditions read the appeal as Zophar’s argument, not as a rule that settles Job’s case.

verses.text: that the triumphing of the wicked is short, the joy of the godless but for a moment?
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar asks whether Job knows “that the triumphing of the wicked is short, the joy of the godless but for a moment.” Arminian readers note that Scripture elsewhere says something similar (cf. Ps 37:1–2).

The principle is true in the long view, but Zophar uses it to imply that Job’s suffering proves guilt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise affirm that God judges the wicked in his time (cf. Ps 73:17).

Shared ground: both traditions agree the statement has general truth, and both note that Job 21 will challenge whether it holds in every life.

verses.text: Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Though his height mount up to the heavens, and his head reach to the clouds.” Arminian readers note the image of pride reaching upward.

The picture recalls warnings against arrogance elsewhere (cf. Isa 14:13–15).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the folly of human exaltation apart from God.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that pride goes before a fall, while recognizing that Zophar is describing a type and applying it to Job without evidence.

verses.text: yet he will perish forever like his own dung. Those who have seen him will say, ‘Where is he?’
verses.arminianNotes:
Zophar says the wicked “will perish forever,” and those who saw him will ask, “Where is he?” Arminian readers note the coarse image Zophar uses for the wicked man’s end.

The point is sudden disappearance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse as Zophar’s vivid way of describing judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions note that Psalm 37:36 speaks of the wicked passing away so that he “could not be found,” and that Zophar presses this truth harshly.

verses.text: He will fly away as a dream, and will not be found. Yes, he will be chased away like a vision of the night.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He will fly away as a dream, and will not be found.” Arminian readers note the image of a life that leaves no lasting trace.

The imagery underscores the brevity Zophar attributes to wicked prosperity.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the transience of a life built without God.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that earthly glory is fleeting (cf. Ps 73:20), and both read the verse as part of Zophar’s argument rather than a description of Job.

verses.text: The eye which saw him will see him no more, neither will his place see him any more.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The eye which saw him will see him no more, neither will his place see him any more.” Arminian readers note the echo of Job’s own words about death (7:8–10).

Zophar applies to the wicked what Job had said of every mortal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the reuse of Job’s language.

Shared ground: both traditions see the friends turning Job’s lament into a description of the wicked, which sharpens the tension of the debate.

verses.text: His children will seek the favor of the poor. His hands will give back his wealth.
verses.arminianNotes:
“His children will seek the favor of the poor. His hands will give back his wealth.” Arminian readers note the reversal: the oppressor’s family becomes dependent on those he wronged.

The theme of restitution is real in Scripture.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see justice reversing the gains of oppression.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God cares for the poor, while noting that Zophar’s words can sound like an indirect charge against Job, whose children have died (1:18–19).

verses.text: His bones are full of his youth, but youth will lie down with him in the dust.
verses.arminianNotes:
“His bones are full of his youth, but youth will lie down with him in the dust.” Arminian readers note the picture of strength cut short.

Zophar insists that vigor offers no protection.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the line as a reminder of mortality.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that all strength ends in the dust, and Job will soon reply that this happens to the righteous and the wicked alike (21:23–26).
